prompt: How would you measure the success of a 'Split the bill' feature in a UPI payments app?

context.setup: You're the PM for payments at a large UPI app.
hiddenFacts: Goal if asked: make group expenses easier so friends keep their shared spending inside our app.
How it works if asked: one person pays the merchant, then sends split requests to friends in the app.
Scale if asked (illustrative): 40 million monthly active users; the feature launched to 10% of them four weeks ago.
Known issue if asked: about a third of split requests are still unpaid after 7 days.
There is no fee today.

expectedStructure: State what the feature is for, and for whom (the payer and the friend who owes)
One north-star metric tied to that goal (for example, splits fully settled within 7 days per active user)
Two or three input metrics along the funnel (created, sent, opened, paid)
A guardrail or counter-metric (unpaid requests, reminder spam, drop in ordinary payments)
How you would read a conflict between metrics, and a target

rubricHints.structure: Goal first, then metrics derived from it; not a list of metric names.
rubricHints.userFocus: Separates the payer's goal (get money back) from the friend's experience (being asked to pay).
rubricHints.prioritisation: Chooses one north star and says why it beats the alternatives.
rubricHints.metrics: Settlement, not creation, is the outcome; names a guardrail and a time window.
rubricHints.communication: Signposted and ends with a one-line summary.

commonPitfalls: App-level NPS for a single feature
Picks a metric because it is easy to move

followUpSeeds.text: How would you catch splits that get created but never paid back?
If you could report only one number to your CEO for this feature, which would it be, and why?
There are two people in every split. Whose success are you measuring?
What target would you set for the first quarter, and where would it come from?
Let's change one thing: {variant}. What changes in how you measure success?

constraint: there is now a ₹2 fee on every split
you can add only one new event to the analytics pipeline
user: the users are flatmates splitting rent every month, not friends splitting dinners
market: the feature is for small shops splitting supplier bills, not consumers

prompt: How would you measure the success of a 'Reorder' button in a grocery delivery app?

context.setup: You're the PM for repeat shoppers at a grocery delivery app.
hiddenFacts: Goal if asked: save repeat shoppers time on their regular basket.
Scale if asked (illustrative): 55% of orders already come from repeat shoppers.
The average basket has 14 items.
The category team is worried that one-tap reorder shrinks baskets and kills discovery of new products.
Reorder launches first in two cities; no fee or discount is attached.

expectedStructure: Say what Reorder is for (time saved for repeat shoppers) and who it helps most
One north-star tied to that goal, for example share of repeat orders placed through Reorder
Input metrics: Reorder taps per repeat shopper, time from app open to checkout
Counter-metrics: basket size, items per order, new-item discovery
How to read a conflict (reorders up, basket down) and a first-quarter target

rubricHints.structure: States the goal before naming metrics and ends on how the numbers will be read together.
rubricHints.userFocus: Separates habitual weekly shoppers from occasional ones and says who Reorder could hurt.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Commits to one north star and says which other metrics are inputs rather than competing goals.
rubricHints.metrics: Defines the north star with population and window; names basket size or discovery as the counter-metric with a direction.
rubricHints.communication: Short, signposted, ends with the single number that decides success.

followUpSeeds.text: If reorders rise 20% but basket size falls 5%, do you ship?
How would you set the target for your north star in the first quarter?
Which single number tells you Reorder is working?
Which shoppers is this for, and who might it hurt?
Let's change one thing: {variant}. What changes in how you measure success?

constraint: the Reorder button can show only five items
user: the shoppers are first-time users with one past order

prompt: You're the PM for 'Communities' in a messaging app. How would you measure its success?

hiddenFacts: Goal if asked: help organisers (schools, housing societies) reach members and keep sub-groups organised.
The feature launched six months ago; admins create a community and link existing groups.
Admins number far fewer than members; most members only read.
Announcements are the most used surface so far.

expectedStructure: Clarify the goal and the two users: admins and members
Value moments for each (admin reaches everyone; member finds what they need)
One primary metric tied to the goal
Supporting adoption and engagement metrics split by user type
Guardrails such as mutes, exits and spam reports

rubricHints.structure: Goal and users first, then value moments, then metrics.
rubricHints.userFocus: Separates admins from members and picks a value moment for each.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Chooses one primary metric and explains why it beats DAU or group count.
rubricHints.metrics: Something like weekly active communities where an announcement reached at least N members, with mute or exit rate as guardrail.
rubricHints.communication: Clear, avoids listing every metric, closes with a one-line summary.

commonPitfalls: Lists DAU/MAU without tying to the goal
Treats admins and members as the same user

followUpSeeds.text: If you could track only one number on a dashboard, which is it and why?
What number would tell you Communities is hurting the rest of the app?
Admins and members get different value. How does your metric reflect both?
Suppose {variant}. Does your primary metric change?

user: the main users are small businesses broadcasting offers to customers
constraint: you cannot read message content and only have counts
market: the market is Brazil, where groups are heavily used for commerce

prompt: How would you measure the success of live order tracking on a food-delivery app?

context.setup: You're the PM for post-order experience at a food-delivery company.
hiddenFacts: Goal if asked: reduce anxiety after ordering and cut 'where is my order' contacts.
About 18% of orders today generate a call or chat to support (illustrative).
Tracking shows a map with the rider's position and an ETA that refreshes every 30 seconds.
Support costs roughly ₹35 per contact (illustrative).

expectedStructure: State the goal: less anxiety and fewer support contacts
Primary metric such as WISMO contacts per 100 orders
Inputs: tracking screen opens per order, ETA accuracy
Guardrails: order cancellations after ordering, ratings, battery or data complaints
Target and how you would test it

rubricHints.structure: Ties each metric back to the stated goal.
rubricHints.userFocus: Notes that anxious first-time orderers behave differently from regulars.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Picks WISMO contacts per order over map opens and says why.
rubricHints.metrics: Contact rate per 100 orders with ETA accuracy as input and cancellation rate as counter-metric.

commonPitfalls: Counts tracking page views as success

followUpSeeds.text: Map opens went up but support contacts did not move. What do you conclude?
Which one of your metrics would you put in front of the head of operations?
What would tell you the tracking screen is making things worse?
Which customers benefit most from live tracking?
Let's change one thing: {variant}. How does your measurement change?

constraint: the ETA is wrong by more than 10 minutes on 30% of orders
user: the customers are people ordering for a family dinner party

prompt: Choose a North Star metric for a music-streaming service in India, and tell me what you'd guard against.

hiddenFacts: Business model if asked: ad-supported free tier plus a premium subscription; most users are free.
Goal: grow paying subscribers while keeping free users engaged for ad revenue.
A large share of listening is regional-language and film music; many users listen on mobile data.
Free-tier ads are capped at one every four songs.

expectedStructure: Clarify business model and current goal
Define the value moment for a listener
Candidate north stars and why one wins (leads revenue, reflects value, movable)
Input metrics teams can move each week
Guardrails and ways the metric could be gamed

rubricHints.structure: Value moment, then north star, then inputs, then guardrails.
rubricHints.userFocus: Distinguishes free and paying listeners and the moments each values.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Explains why the chosen metric beats subscribers or DAU.
rubricHints.metrics: Something like weekly listeners with at least N minutes of intentional listening; names skips, churn or ad load as guardrails.
rubricHints.communication: Defends the choice crisply under challenge.

commonPitfalls: Picks revenue as the north star
Ignores the free versus paid split

followUpSeeds.text: Why not just use paid subscribers as the North Star?
What are the two or three input metrics your teams would actually move each week?
How could a team game your North Star in a way that hurts the business?
Now {variant}. Would you change the North Star?

prompt: What North Star metric would you choose for an exam-preparation app for Class 10 students?

rubricHints.structure: Starts from the learning outcome and works toward a measurable proxy.
rubricHints.userFocus: Separates the student's use from the parent's payment decision.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Rejects minutes in app and DAU for stated reasons.
rubricHints.metrics: Defines action, population and window; adds a guardrail such as accuracy decay or refund rate.

commonPitfalls: Time spent as the North Star

followUpSeeds.text: Why is minutes per user a poor North Star here?

prompt: Define the North Star metric for a B2B app that helps kirana store owners reorder stock from distributors.

context.setup: You're the PM at a startup serving about 80,000 neighbourhood stores.
hiddenFacts: Revenue comes from a small margin on orders placed through the app.
Typical store reorders every 4 to 7 days, many by phone call to the distributor's sales rep today.

expectedStructure: Clarify the goal (retention of stores versus GMV versus margin)
Value moment: store restocks faster or cheaper without a phone call
North star such as weekly stores placing at least one order, or share of a store's restocking done in-app
Inputs: catalogue availability, price competitiveness, delivery reliability
Guardrails: credit defaults, order fill rate, margin

rubricHints.structure: Chooses the north star from the value moment, then decomposes it.
rubricHints.userFocus: Treats the store owner (low app time, high stakes per order) as the user and notes the distributor rep as another stakeholder.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Argues for share of wallet or weekly active ordering stores over raw GMV.
rubricHints.metrics: Defines population and window and adds fill rate and credit default as guardrails.
rubricHints.communication: Keeps the metric simple enough to explain to a store owner.

followUpSeeds.text: GMV is growing fast. Why would you not use it as the North Star?

Which stores are you optimising for first, and why?

prompt: Payments on your UPI app earn no revenue. What North Star would you pick, and how does it connect to a business that pays for itself?

hiddenFacts: Peer-to-peer and merchant UPI payments carry zero MDR today.

prompt: An A/B test of a new checkout page on a fashion e-commerce app shows +4% conversion but −6% average order value. Do you ship it?

hiddenFacts: The test ran 7 days, including a sale weekend; roughly 200k users per arm.
Conversion lift is significant (p about 0.01); the order value drop is significant (p about 0.04).
Revenue per visitor is roughly −2% if the candidate asks or computes it.
The new page removed the 'add ₹300 more for free shipping' nudge.
Return-rate data is not yet available because it lags 30 days.

expectedStructure: Clarify the goal metric (revenue per visitor, profit, new buyers)
Combine conversion and order value into revenue per visitor
Check test validity: duration, sale weekend, novelty, sample ratio
Diagnose the order value drop (removed free-shipping nudge)
Decide with conditions: do not ship as is; restore the nudge and retest, or ship to a segment

rubricHints.userFocus: Notes new versus repeat buyers may react differently.
rubricHints.prioritisation: Makes a clear decision with conditions instead of 'it depends'.
rubricHints.metrics: Combines conversion and AOV into revenue per visitor and mentions margin or returns.
rubricHints.communication: States the decision first, then the reason.

followUpSeeds.text: Put the two numbers together. Is the business better or worse off per visitor?

rubricHints.metrics: Argues opens are a proxy; uses orders per user and retention as the real outcomes.
